title: 401(k)s & the Employer Match
description: The percent of pay, the tax door, and the match you do not want to skip.
wolfLine: The match is pay. Raise the rate until you have all of it.

roth-401k.definition: A 401(k) you fund with pay that has already been taxed. Qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free. It is not a Roth IRA, and it does not use the Roth IRA income limit.
roth-401k.example: Choosing the Roth option inside the workplace plan for $1,000 of pay.

lessons.title: The Contribution Rate
lessons.summary: A percent of pay, every paycheck.

steps.title: The percent
steps.body: The contribution rate is the slice of pay that goes into the [[401(k)|401k]] before you see it. Jamie, from the earning section, earns $52,000 and currently sends 4%. This employer matches 50 cents per dollar you put in, up to 6% of pay. That match is this plan’s rule, not a law.

steps.prompt: Jamie earns $52,000 and contributes 4%. How many dollars a year is that?
The match is 50% of what Jamie puts in, and 4% is under the 6% cap. How many match dollars is that?
steps.explain: 0.50 × $2,080 = $1,040. The plan will not match past 6% of pay.

steps.prompt: To get the full match, Jamie needs to contribute 6%. How many dollars a year is 6% of $52,000?
steps.explain: 0.06 × $52,000 = $3,120. The match on that would be half, $1,560.

steps.prompt: The employer match is required by law to be 50% up to 6%.
steps.explain: This lesson uses one plan’s rule. Another employer can match more, less, or nothing. Read your plan.

lessons.title: Traditional or Roth 401(k)
lessons.summary: The tax break now, or the tax break later.

steps.title: Same plan, two tax doors
steps.body: A traditional [[401(k)|401k]] contribution is a [[pre-tax deduction|pre-tax-deduction]]. In the 12% bracket, $1,000 contributed saves $120 of tax this year. A [[Roth 401(k)|roth-401k]] uses pay that was already taxed, so this year saves $0. Qualified Roth withdrawals later are tax-free. Neither door is a Roth IRA.

docs.title: Traditional 401(k)
docs.subtitle: Pre-tax. Taxable pay falls by $1,000.

lines.label: Tax saved this year in the 12% bracket

docs.note: The withdrawal in retirement is taxed.

docs.title: Roth 401(k)
docs.subtitle: After-tax. No break this year.
docs.note: Qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax-free.

steps.prompt: Which page lowers this year’s taxable pay?
steps.explain: The traditional page is the pre-tax one. $1,000 × 0.12 = $120 saved this year. The Roth page takes the tax break later, if the withdrawal is qualified.

steps.prompt: In the 12% bracket, how many dollars of tax does a $1,000 traditional contribution save this year?
steps.explain: $1,000 × 0.12 = $120. A $1,000 Roth contribution saves $0 this year.

steps.prompt: A Roth 401(k) uses the same income limit as a Roth IRA.
steps.explain: The Roth IRA income limit is for the IRA. A Roth 401(k), if your plan offers it, does not use that limit.

steps.prompt: You expect a higher tax bracket in retirement than the 12% you pay now. Which door takes the tax at today’s lower rate?
choices: Roth, which pays the tax now
Neither, because 401(k) money is never taxed
steps.explain: Roth pays now, at the current rate, and a qualified withdrawal later is tax-free. Traditional does the reverse. This is a sketch, not advice for your bracket.

lessons.title: The Plan Menu
lessons.summary: A short list. Read the fee and the bet.

steps.title: You do not need all four
steps.body: A 401(k) menu is a list the plan picked. A broad [[index fund]] with a tiny [[expense ratio]] is usually the workhorse. Your employer’s own stock can show a $0 fee and still be [[concentration risk]], because your paycheck already depends on that company.

doc.title: Plan menu, fees on $10,000
doc.subtitle: Four choices. The $0 fee is not the safe one.

lines.label: US stock index fund, yearly fee
International stock index fund, yearly fee
Your employer’s own stock, yearly fee

doc.note: Fees are the expense ratio turned into dollars on $10,000.

steps.prompt: On $10,000, how many dollars a year does the US stock index fund cost?
steps.explain: The US stock index line is $4. That is a 0.04% expense ratio on $10,000.

steps.prompt: Which line is a single company, even though the fee is $0?
steps.explain: A $0 fee does not fix concentration. The job and the stock are the same company.

steps.prompt: You should buy every fund on the menu so none of them feel left out.
steps.explain: The menu is a list of options. A few broad, cheap funds can cover the mix. More names is not more of a plan.

steps.prompt: How many more dollars a year is the international index fund than the US stock index fund, on this $10,000?
steps.explain: $6 − $4 = $2. Both are cheap. The employer stock is the odd line, not the $2.

steps.title: The slow raise
steps.body: Auto-escalation raises your contribution rate a little each year, often 1 percentage point, until you hit a cap you chose. Jamie is at 4%. A 1-point raise makes it 5%. On $52,000 that is $520 more of Jamie’s money, plus more match.

steps.prompt: Jamie goes from 4% to 5% of $52,000. How many more dollars a year does Jamie contribute?
steps.explain: 1% of $52,000 = $520. The new contribution is $2,600.

steps.prompt: The match is 50% and 5% is still under the 6% match cap. How many extra match dollars does that $520 bring?
How many new dollars, Jamie’s plus the match, go in because of that one-point raise?
Auto-escalation means the plan invests 100% of your pay next year.
steps.explain: It nudges the rate, often by 1 point a year. You can usually opt out or pick the cap.

lessons.title: The 2026 Limits
lessons.summary: The employee cap, then the age add-on.

steps.title: Whose limit
steps.body: In 2026 the employee [[401(k)|401k]] deferral limit is $24,500. That is your money, not the match. At age 50 the catch-up is $8,000 more, for a total of $32,500. At ages 60 through 63 the catch-up is $11,250, for a total of $35,750. Jamie is 23, so Jamie gets the $24,500 cap and not the catch-up. These are IRS figures for 2026.

steps.prompt: What is the 2026 employee 401(k) deferral limit, in dollars, before any catch-up?
steps.explain: The 2026 employee cap is $24,500. The match can sit on top. Jamie’s $2,080 is under the cap.

steps.prompt: At age 50 in 2026, what is the total employee deferral including the $8,000 catch-up?
At age 61 in 2026, what is the total employee deferral including the $11,250 catch-up?
steps.explain: $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750. That higher catch-up is only for ages 60 through 63.

steps.prompt: Jamie, at 23, can use the age-50 catch-up.
steps.explain: The catch-up is an age rule. 23 gets the $24,500 base limit only.

lessons.title: A Loan from the Plan
lessons.summary: Your money leaves the market, and the job can call it due.

steps.title: Borrowing from yourself
steps.body: Some plans let you borrow from the [[401(k)|401k]]. A $5,000 loan is $5,000 that is not invested while you repay it. Leave the job and the loan often comes due quickly. Miss that, and it can be treated as a withdrawal: income tax, plus the usual 10% penalty if you are under 59½. It is a last resort, not a clever trick.

steps.prompt: How many dollars are out of the market during a $5,000 plan loan?
steps.explain: The $5,000 is no longer invested. Repayments put money back over time. The missed growth is the quiet cost.

steps.prompt: Quitting the job usually leaves a 401(k) loan quietly in place for decades.
steps.explain: Leaving often makes the loan due. Unpaid, it can become a taxable withdrawal, with a penalty if you are under 59½.

steps.prompt: What is the strongest reason to avoid a 401(k) loan for a want, not an emergency?
choices: The money stays invested the whole time
The money leaves the market, and the job can turn the loan into a taxable withdrawal
steps.explain: Two costs: time out of the market, and a bill that can show up when you leave.

steps.prompt: The 10% early-withdrawal penalty, if the unpaid loan is treated as a withdrawal, generally applies before what age?
steps.explain: Before 59½, an early withdrawal from a traditional 401(k) is usually tax plus a 10% penalty. Some exceptions exist. Do not plan on them.

lessons.title: When the Match Is Yours
lessons.summary: Your dollars are yours. Theirs may have a clock.

steps.title: A clock on their money
steps.body: [[Vesting]] is earning the [[employer match]] over time. Your own contributions are yours from day one. This example plan vests 25% of the match for each full year you stay. That schedule is an example, like the one in the earning section. Your plan document is the real one.

steps.prompt: The match so far is $2,000 and you are 50% vested. How many match dollars are yours?
steps.explain: 0.50 × $2,000 = $1,000. The other $1,000 goes back if you leave now.

steps.prompt: You contributed $4,000 of your own pay. How many of those dollars are yours, vesting aside?
steps.explain: Your contributions are not on the vesting clock. All $4,000 is yours.

steps.prompt: You leave after the example plan has vested 25% of a $2,000 match. How many match dollars do you keep?
steps.explain: 25% of $2,000 is $500. Your own contributions still leave with you.

steps.prompt: Vesting applies to the money you put in yourself.
steps.explain: Vesting is about the employer’s money. Yours is yours.

lessons.title: Jamie Turns It Up
lessons.summary: One point a year, toward the full match.

story.title: One point
story.body:
Jamie earns **$52,000** and puts **4%** into the 401(k), which is **$2,080**. This plan matches 50% up to 6% of pay, so the full match would be **$1,560**. Jamie is getting **$1,040**.

A 1% auto-escalation makes next year’s rate **5%**.

steps.title: Meet Jamie, a year along
steps.body:
Jamie is 23, in that first salaried job at $52,000. The 401(k) is at 4%, which is $2,080, and the match on it is $1,040. The plan matches 50% up to 6% of pay, so the full match is $1,560.

Jamie turns on a 1% auto-escalation. Next year the rate is 5%, if the pay stays $52,000.

steps.prompt: How many match dollars is Jamie missing by contributing 4% instead of 6%?
steps.explain: The full match is $1,560. Jamie is getting $1,040. $1,560 − $1,040 = $520 left on the table.

steps.prompt: After the one-point raise, Jamie contributes 5%. How many dollars a year is that?
Jamie should skip the match to pick individual stocks in the plan.
steps.explain: The match is part of pay. The menu’s broad, cheap funds can hold it. Single stocks are the concentration.

steps.prompt: Put Jamie’s raise in order.
items: Get the plan’s match rule in writing
Raise the rate by 1 point, from 4% to 5%
Let the next year’s raise move it toward 6%
Leave the investments in broad, cheap funds
steps.explain: The match rule first, then the slow raise, then the fund choice. 6% is where this plan’s match stops growing.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: 401(k)s & the Employer Match
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: In 2026, what is the employee 401(k) deferral limit before any age catch-up?
steps.explain: The 2026 employee cap is $24,500. Catch-up amounts are extra, and only at the ages the IRS names.

steps.prompt: A plan matches 50% up to 6% of a $40,000 salary. The worker contributes 6%. How many match dollars is that?
steps.explain: 6% of $40,000 is $2,400. Half of that is $1,200.

steps.prompt: Your own 401(k) contributions vest on the same clock as the employer match.
steps.explain: Your contributions are yours. Vesting is the clock on the match.

steps.prompt: A Roth 401(k) contribution does what to this year’s taxable pay?
choices: Lowers it, like a traditional contribution
Does not lower it, because the money was already taxed
steps.explain: Roth is the after-tax door. The traditional door is the one that lowers taxable pay now.
